title: How to do pull-ups to maximize muscle growth and minimize injury risks
summary: NH demonstrates hypertrophy pull-ups: learn scapular retraction from a dead hang, start from the top, use a controlled negative, and work in a 'striking range' that never lets the lats disengage at the bottom. He explains why locked-out rebounding causes elbow and tendon pain, rotates many grips to do 40-60 weighted pull-ups daily, and argues the back can take huge volume.
claims: Pull-ups are one of the most essential movement patterns for a big, aesthetic natural back
He neglected pull-ups in the past and ended up with a small back
For hypertrophy, do pull-ups with a measured range of motion, a controlled negative and the intent to pull with the back, not the arms
Many people pull only with their arms because they focus on getting up at any cost, and get little back growth for years
Before doing pull-ups, practise dead-hang scapular retractions (engage/disengage) to build a relationship with the lats
Scapular engage/disengage drills can be done without a bar, all day, as a game
Advanced trainees should pre-squeeze the scapulae and start from the top with a negative so the lats are already engaged
Going so deep that the lats disengage, or sacrificing reps to get as high as possible, both miss the point
The striking range, from just above the bottom (lats stretched but engaged) to partway up, is the most beneficial for hypertrophy because the lat works hardest there
Dangling at the bottom gives no benefit and disengages the scapula, so later reps become arm-dominated rebounds
Eight reps in the striking range beat four full-range reps
Go slow on the negative because time under tension matters: six slow reps beat six fast ones, without being exaggeratedly slow
Calisthenics are easy on the body but bad pull-up technique still causes problems; injuries are the main limiter for most people
Elbow, shoulder and biceps tendon problems from pull-ups mostly come from overextending the arms at the bottom and rebounding, sending force through the arms while the back is disengaged
Keep a slight elbow bend at the bottom; a full dead hang is a separate lift that is good for tendons as long as you do not rebound out of it
He does 40-60 weighted pull-ups every day and never has tendon pain
Rotating grips (neutral, chin-up, pronated, wide, narrow, fat grips, towels) prevents overuse injury and is why he can do pull-ups daily
Beginners should pick one or two grips, pronated and chin-ups for most, then expand
Giving yourself grip variety keeps pull-ups exciting if you get bored of them
Progressively overloading pull-up reps over 10 years will make your back look ridiculous
Most people underestimate how much volume the back can take; training it once or twice a week explains small backs
Pull-ups done this way are almost purely back with only a small biceps contribution on chin-ups, so you can feed the back huge volume
More advanced lifters can lean back and pull higher, trying to touch the chest to the bar
exercises: hang, retract and depress the scapulae, release, repeat
builds the mind-muscle connection with the lats
start at the top, pre-squeeze scapulae, slow negative, stop with slight elbow bend, pull from the back
maximises lat tension and spares tendons
good for tendons but a separate lift from pull-ups
recommended with pronated pull-ups for beginners
grip variations that load forearms more
